item.title: Confronting and Letting Go of Toxic Shame
item.description:
Some of us grew up in families where we felt invisible and unimportant, regardless of what we tried to do to get attention and affection. Some of us had terrible experiences with people who should have loved and protected us, but instead hurt us and exploited us. Some of us were bullied, rejected, and ridiculed for things that we couldn’t help, by peers or by people old enough to know better. The painful memories from these experiences stayed with us in the form of toxic shame.

Toxic shame hides in our hearts. It tells us that we’re not good enough, that there is something wrong with us, that we’ll never amount to anything more than what we are now. It may even tell us that we are fundamentally unlovable.

These are sentences that we don’t necessarily hear. They are ideas and beliefs that we probably don’t repeat out loud, but they still affect our self-image. These are the beliefs that lie at our foundation, brought into being by the shame surrounding our most painful experiences.

At some point, though, we will encounter the opposite of what we’re used to. We will meet someone who wants to accept us, to cherish us, to love us, and to enjoy our company. When this happens, we will have no choice but to confront the toxic shame that shields us from accepting this love, and to heal it from the inside out. There is a long life ahead of us, filled with wonderful opportunities, but to advance, we must heal the hurt that lies beneath toxic shame.

We Accept the Love We Think We Deserve

Everyone has a baseline of the kind of treatment they think they deserve, and this is called our norm. It is our past experiences, both painful and positive, that determine our norms. When we get less than what we are used to, or when we are treated below our level of norm, our default emotion is anger. Imagine receiving your monthly paycheck, and it is significantly less than you are used to receiving each month. You will feel disbelief, you will want an explanation, and you will be outraged at the injustice of getting less than what you are used to.

When we get more than our norm, and when we have toxic shame, our response is guilt.

If someone else looked at their monthly paycheck and noticed significantly more money there than they are used to, they might also respond with disbelief. When they followed up about it and discovered that the amount was not a mistake, they would be delighted and grateful.

The person with toxic shame in this same scenario, however, would feel guilty and unworthy. They would reflect on their failures and human moments, and they would think of these moments as the reasons why they are disqualified from getting a pay raise.

Everyone evaluates their self-worth based on the way they were treated in their earliest memories, to the way they were treated through their childhood and teen years. The way others treated them dictates their value and sets the baseline norm of how they expect to be treated.

If they were neglected, abused, mistreated, or bullied, they will carry toxic shame as if they were to blame for those experiences. Their baseline norm for receiving love is low, and they feel guilty or ashamed each time they receive more love or when they are treated kinder than they are used to. This is what the phrase “We accept the love we think we deserve” truly means.

People who carry toxic shame purposely make it difficult for others to love them. In the Bible, we are told that Adam and Eve had a close friendship with their Creator, and the author even tells us that they were naked and had no shame. As soon as they do what they were told not to do, they become aware of their nakedness, they cover themselves, and they withdraw from God, hiding from Him as He comes to look for them. (Genesis 3)

Adam and Eve covering up, withdrawing, and hiding is a perfect picture of what toxic shame does to us. We put up emotional barriers and create distance from those looking to connect with us because we feel unworthy, exposed, or broken beyond repair.

Letting Go of Toxic Shame

Many of us spend our lives oblivious to our emotions and the thoughts behind them. Similar to the physical foundations of a building, we all have unseen thoughts and beliefs that form the foundation of our identity; it is the essence of how we feel about ourselves. A teacher might have scolded us in front of the class, telling us that we’re hopeless because we never listen to instructions. That simple sentence might go on to form the foundation of our identity, magnifying one of our struggles to the point that it becomes a defining feature.

Some of us were never told anything in our young lives, positive or negative. We were left alone for vast stretches of time, our achievements unnoticed, our needs unmet, and our painful emotions ignored. Neglected children grow up believing that they are unlovable and unworthy of praise, based on the affection that they never received.

This is toxic shame because it causes someone to feel guilty even when they were a victim. The same goes for children who were mistreated and abused. They carry toxic shame as if they caused bad things to happen to them.

It’s not simple, but it is possible to heal and release toxic shame. We are spiritual beings in a physical body, with minds and emotions. We must learn to reach and speak to every part of ourselves, leaving no broken area unaddressed. There are physical exercises that heal our nervous system, and there are affirmations to speak to our damaged mind and emotions. God has spoken loving truths to our spirits, and we must hear them and accept them to be healed within.

The further we go into dealing with our past and toxic shame, the more we will realize that some things are impossible to do alone. Many of us were hurt by others, and those same hurts can only be healed by others, as uncomfortable and scary as that idea might be.

One of the central parts of healing toxic shame lies in learning to become vulnerable with others, in the way God wanted Adam and Eve to be vulnerable with Him. Not everyone can be trusted, but we must find the ones who can. Healing will only come when we allow others to see our shame and love us anyway.

You might look at yourself in the mirror now and struggle to comprehend how anyone could love you. You have never needed to earn love, and you have never needed to make yourself lovable. Toxic shame has had you believing all kinds of things about yourself that have never been true.

It can be scary and deeply uncomfortable to confront your past and to let go of the beliefs you have been clinging to. It is only when you can let go of the handfuls of shame that you have been holding that you can have a free hand to receive and accept the love that you have always been deserving of and that the people around you have been desperate for you to receive.

Perhaps you don’t have someone that you can trust with details of your past. When you speak with a counselor, you are in a safe place, with someone who will keep your confidence. You can meet with as many counselors as it takes for you to feel safe and comfortable enough to open up to the right person. To get started, please consult our online catalog of counselors or speak with our reception team. We trust that you will find someone and begin the healing process soon.

item.title: Self-Care for Depression: Small Changes that Can Help Improve Your Mood
item.description:
Self-care involves taking proper care of your daily needs, such as eating, sleeping, and personal hygiene. However, depression can drain your energy and make it hard to find the strength or motivation to do so. Just thinking about taking care of yourself may feel like an unattainable challenge. The result is a vicious cycle where the worse you feel, the less you do, and the less you do, the worse you feel.

This is because depression is more than a mindset problem. It is a mood disorder that involves changes in brain chemistry and nervous system regulation, zaps energy and motivation, distorts thinking, makes everything feel harder than it should, and makes activities that would lift your mood, such as self-care, feel pointless.

As a result, self-care for depression tends to be a difficult, counterintuitive process of doing the things that help even when you do not feel like doing them.

Habits that Fuel Depression

Small automatic daily habits you may not even be consciously aware of tend to add up over time, shaping your moods, leading you to feel mentally and emotionally overwhelmed, and fueling the symptoms of depression. The good news, however, is that if you learn to recognize these habits, you can take steps to unlearn them.

Discounting the positive Constantly discounting positivity, expecting the worst, dismissing wins, and rejecting compliments trains your brain to ignore the good and focus only on the negative.

Self-criticism Judging and berating yourself for the way you feel instead of accepting your emotions and criticizing yourself for all the things you do not do fuels shame and inaction.

Numbing behaviors Trying not to feel bad by numbing your feelings through distracting yourself or turning to food or alcohol may provide temporary relief from emotional pain, but tends to make your depression worse in the long run.

Rumination Ruminating on the past and replaying mistakes, perceived failures, injustices, or what could have been only keeps you stuck and deepens your depression.

Cognitive distortions Using emotional reasoning and allowing cognitive distortions such as all-or-nothing thinking to convince you that nothing you do will help or work creates unreasonable standards and reinforces feelings of worthlessness and hopelessness.

Self-neglect Using fatigue as an excuse to avoid self-care or engaging with others causes your energy to drop even lower and makes it even harder to do the things that can help you feel better.

Isolating Withdrawing from life to avoid difficult situations and isolating from others to avoid being hurt reinforces false beliefs of worthlessness and deprives you of the positive interactions and emotional support needed to help regulate your mood.

Waiting to feel motivated Waiting to feel motivated before taking action can become an easy trap to get stuck in that keeps you from taking any action at all.

Small Daily Practices that Can Help Improve Your Mood

The following are some simple evidence-based self-care practices that can help you break the inertia caused by depression and improve your mood. Strive for consistency rather than perfection.

Prioritize quality sleep Not getting enough sleep worsens symptoms of depression, whereas healthy sleep habits can lift your mood, improve brain function, and increase your level of energy.

To help facilitate good sleep, create and stick to a consistent sleep schedule, going to bed and getting up at the same time each day; have a calming bedtime routine; keep your bedroom cool, quiet, and dark; avoid caffeine late in the day; and limit screen time for a couple of hours before bed.

Create structure in your day Creating structure in your day by establishing a simple daily routine with small, realistic, achievable goals such as getting up at a certain time; eating three balanced meals; and completing simple tasks like making your bed, taking out the trash, or loading the dishwasher can add shape and direction to the day, provide a sense of control and predictability, and help combat lack of motivation.

Pay attention to your thoughts Depression changes the way your brain processes information, and thoughts like “nothing will ever change” or “I can’t do anything right” can feel like facts that, over time, reinforce feelings such as hopelessness.

When you notice yourself having these thoughts, stop and question them rather than accepting them as reality. Ask yourself whether there is any evidence to support that conclusion, or if there is an alternate, more balanced, realistic way of looking at it.

Journal Journaling can help you release painful emotions and overwhelming feelings by getting them out of your head and onto paper, where you can process them without trying to fix them. It can also help you track mood patterns and what seems to influence them, as well as identify, challenge, and reframe habitual negative thoughts.

Practice gratitude Write down three things you are grateful for when you get up in the morning, or before you go to bed at night. Making a habit of looking for small joys and positives as you go about your day can help boost your mood, as well as retrain your brain by redirecting its focus to small daily accomplishments and things you are thankful for.

Move your body Studies have shown that regular physical activity can significantly reduce symptoms of depression by lowering levels of the stress hormone cortisol and boosting the release of feel-good chemicals such as endorphins.

You don’t have to engage in an intense workout or anything strenuous. Even light physical activity such as walking, stretching, or gardening can give your mood and energy a boost. Small amounts add up. Find something you enjoy, make it part of your daily routine, and aim for consistency and regularity.

Spend time in nature Spending time outdoors in the fresh air and sunlight can have a positive impact on your mood. 30 minutes daily not only has a mood-lifting effect; it also supports vitamin D synthesis and circadian regulation.

Set screen time boundaries How you engage online matters. Active engagement, such as creating content or connecting with others in a meaningful way, can be positive, whereas passive engagement like endless scrolling tends to worsen symptoms of depression. Set boundaries for yourself, such as limiting the time you spend on social media, not bringing your phone to the table at mealtime, and avoiding screen time for at least an hour before bedtime.

Practice grounding techniques Grounding techniques, such as deep breathing or mindfulness exercises that use your five senses to center you in the present moment, help reduce the physical symptoms of depression and interrupt the process of rehashing the past or worrying about the future

Eat a healthy diet What you eat affects your mood. Eating a healthy diet rich in fruits, vegetables, healthy fats, leafy greens, whole grains, and lean protein, and staying hydrated, can help lift and stabilize your mood.

Connect with others Depression makes you want to withdraw from social contact, but lack of social contact worsens the symptoms of depression. Reach out to someone you trust and tell them how you are feeling, or join a support group where you can connect with others facing similar struggles and who can relate to what you are going through,

Do one thing you enjoy every day Make a habit of doing one thing every day that you used to enjoy, even if you don’t feel like doing it.

Be kind to yourself Be kind to yourself, and treat yourself with the same compassion you would extend to a friend. Instead of berating yourself for things you could not do, acknowledge the efforts you made and the things you accomplished – however small.

If you have questions about this article on self-care for depression or need more help than it could provide, please do not hesitate to give us a call.

item.title: The Unquiet Mind: Finding Support for Nighttime Anxiety
item.description:
There’s something about the dark that strips away the distractions, and during the day, with a packed schedule, a phone full of notifications, and a relentless to-do list, the noise keeps moving fast enough that deeper worries stay in the background.

Nighttime anxiety has a way of surfacing everything that the daylight hours help push aside. The room is quiet, and the mind gets loud. Many individuals find that this is when the fear, dread, and rumination settle in like unwelcome guests. No amount of exhaustion seems to make the anxiety move out so that sleep can move in. This is an experience that goes deeper than a habit of overthinking, and it affects far more people than most would expect.

The psalmist wrote from that same place – needing rest and finding it not through effort, but through trusting God.

In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O Lord, make me dwell in safety. – Psalm 4:8, ESV

The Mind That Won’t Slow Down

The mind was not designed to simply switch off at bedtime. What unfolds during the night is often a continuation of what the brain has been processing all day, except now it is without buffers.

Societal expectations, unfinished conversations, and fears about the future compete for space in a mind that is depleted but not yet rested. This results in a cycle that feels impossible to break. The more an individual tries to force themselves to sleep, the more alert the brain becomes, and this alertness leaves more room for worry to expand.

Prevailing attitudes toward stress management often center on productivity and positive thinking, leaving little room for what happens in the dark. Individuals are told to decompress, meditate, and develop better routines as if anxiety simply responds to instruction.

The mind doesn’t follow a schedule, and nighttime hours are often when the body finally reckons with what has been set aside all day. For many, it is the first real moment of stillness in hours – and stillness, without the proper foundation, can feel more threatening than restful.

Christian counselors recognize this kind of internal reckoning – and they understand it is not a sign of weakness. It is, in many cases, the beginning of genuine healing.

Nighttime Anxiety and the Stories People Tell Themselves

One of the hardest things about lying awake with anxiety is the narrative that forms in the silence. It’s no surprise that the mind tends to reach for worst-case scenarios after dark – the health concern that becomes a diagnosis, the financial worry that becomes a catastrophe, the relational dilemma that becomes permanent loss.

These are stories built on fear, and the late-night hours provide a stage where they can feel entirely convincing. Without external input, they have room to grow and deepen well beyond what the waking hours would allow.

This kind of anxious thinking frequently follows a specific pattern: a thought enters, the body responds with a physical stress reaction, and the thought grows larger in response to that signal. Anxiety and sleep disruption are closely interconnected, feeding each other in a loop that becomes harder to interrupt the longer it continues.

Just because an individual understands this cycle doesn’t mean it will not automatically break – but it does begin to shift the relationship a person has with his or her own thoughts. This understanding introduces the possibility that what feels overwhelmingly true at two in the morning is not necessarily the full picture of reality.

Scripture offers an anchor that is more stabilizing than perspective:

You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you. – Isaiah 26:3, ESV

Learning to return to that anchor in the middle of the night is a practice worth developing.

What the Body Carries Into the Night

Anxiety is not just a mental experience. It is also deeply physical. The body tends to hold the day’s stress in ways that are not visible until the demands of wakefulness are removed. Elevated cortisol levels and a heightened nervous system can cause nighttime symptoms, such as restlessness, muscle tightness, or an inability to settle into stillness.

It is for these reasons that an approach must address more than the mind; it must also include the body. Practices such as slow, intentional breathing, deliberate muscle relaxation, and grounding techniques can signal to an overactive nervous system that it is safe to settle.

These are not instant solutions, but over time, they offer a meaningful starting point for releasing what the body has been carrying throughout the day.

Chronic stress and sleep disruption can become embedded in the nervous system, which makes genuine relaxation difficult even in safe environments. This is a physiological response to sustained pressure and is one of the reasons why professional support will make a meaningful difference.

Christian counselors are trained to address both the emotional and physical dimensions of anxiety, recognizing that the person seeking help is not just a collection of thoughts. They are a body, a soul, and a spirit navigating something real. Jesus extended a direct invitation for this kind of exhaustion:

Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. – Matthew 11:28, ESV

Navigating Nighttime Anxiety Through Faith and Support

Just because an individual has faith does not mean he or she will not experience anxiety. But faith offers a foundation that remains stable even when the mind is not. This allows the individual to bring fear into an honest conversation with God instead of trying to manage it alone in the dark.

Developing practices that return the nervous system to a place of safety through surrender is itself a form of healing. Prayer, Scripture, and intentional breathing serve as anchors in the late-night hours when the mind continues to spiral.

Professional support becomes essential when anxiety persists, deepens, and begins to affect daily functioning. When someone works with Christian counselors, they find a space where the clinical and the spiritual dimensions of anxiety are held together. It is in this space that they can examine the thoughts that surface in the night and understand the patterns beneath them. The result is the development of real tools for moving through nighttime anxiety.

Faith and professional care are not competing approaches. Together, they reinforce each other in powerful ways. Scripture reminds believers not to be anxious about anything, but to bring every request to God through prayer and thanksgiving – and the peace that follows surpasses all understanding (Philippians 4:6–7, ESV).

The Night Does Not Have the Final Word

The hours after midnight can feel like the loneliest place to be – especially when the rest of the world is asleep, and the mind is running its own quiet marathon. In those hours, it becomes easy to believe that what an individual is experiencing is uniquely theirs and that no one else will grapple with these particular fears in these particular hours.

The reality is that this experience is shared among many, connecting more people than the silence would suggest. Those who carry their faith into the dark hours find something profound in the knowledge that God is not absent from the night. He knows what surfaces when everything else is still; He is present in it and steady when nothing else seems to be.

Healing from anxiety is a process that deserves real investment. It involves understanding how the mind works and giving the body what it needs to release accumulated stress. Sometimes it requires support from people who are equipped to walk alongside the fears that surface in the dark.

For many, simply naming what surfaces at night and bringing it into an honest counseling relationship is where real movement begins. This journey calls for patience – and the willingness to cast every anxiety at the feet of the One who already carries them.

If you or a loved one has found that nights have become a source of fear rather than rest, support is available. Reach out to our reception team to get connected with support that can help you navigate nighttime anxiety from a place of faith.

item.title: How to Give Effective Support to a Depressed Person
item.description:
It is never easy to witness the suffering of others. That is even more so when the person who is struggling is someone you care about. You sympathize with them and feel as if you have taken on some of their burden.

When it comes to giving effective support to a depressed person, it can be a challenging, emotional, and deeply meaningful goal. Not only do you need patience, empathy, and wisdom, but it is also important to be physically and emotionally present for them without losing yourself in the process.

How Best to Support a Depressed Loved One

As you consider how best to support a depressed loved one, it is important to consider how best to position yourself for that role. While it may be easy to jump in feet first to help a loved one, it is not wise to do so when you do not know what is going on or how best to help.

Some of the things to consider before you proceed to be a support to a depressed loved one include the following:

Wield your influence well One of the things to consider before providing support to a depressed loved one is that you have limits and/or boundaries. It is wise to know your boundaries and work well within them. It is good to encourage and model healthy routines like getting good rest, getting exercise, and eating well. You can reinforce hope and connection by reminding your loved one of their value and worth as an individual created and loved by God.

Part of wielding your influence also includes being a support for them to get professional care. You can help them research options for therapy and even take them to their appointments.

Avoid dysfunction or codependency You cannot cure your loved one’s depression. Your role is one of offering support. Set healthy boundaries and say “No” if you start feeling overwhelmed. You should maintain your own commitments, hobbies, and other friendships. Setting a boundary does not mean that you are withdrawing your love from your loved one.

You can also encourage your loved one’s independence by guiding them to manage their own wellness journey instead of doing everything for them. These activities or commitments need to be communicated honestly so that you prevent any miscommunications that might arise.

It is also wise to know how and when to step back. If it comes to a place where your support enables your loved one to avoid therapy or their responsibilities, it may be time to reevaluate your participation. Recognize the limits of your role, because you are not your loved one’s therapist or savior. While your support is valuable, it is not a cure-all. Depression is a serious mental health and psychological condition that requires professional help.

Care for yourself, too Supporting a loved one with depression is a challenge. In order to provide effective support, you also need to care for yourself. That includes setting emotional limits and knowing when you need a break to prevent burnout. Setting limits also helps you maintain balance in your own life and reduces the risk of becoming resentful.

Caring for yourself also includes seeking your own support. Find a trusted friend, family member, or therapist so that your needs are also met. Prioritize rest and good sleep, eating healthy, and activities that recharge your batteries. It is wise to educate yourself about depression. Understanding what depression is helps you to respond both compassionately and effectively on behalf of your loved one.

Giving Effective Support to a Depressed Person

As you consider how to give effective support to a loved one dealing with depression, it is important to consider how to position yourself so that you can be of effective help. Some of the ways you can support a loved one struggling with depression include the following:

Recognize the signs. Depression is a mood disorder that affects an individual’s thinking, how they feel, and the way they act. When you know the signs, you can urge your loved one to get the help they need sooner. The signs of depression include persistent sadness, irritability, excessive guilt and self-blame, hopelessness, and a loss of interest in hobbies and activities they once enjoyed.

Some behavioral signs to be alert to include your loved one’s neglect of their responsibilities, withdrawing from loved ones or social activities, immersing themselves in work, and significant changes in their eating and sleeping habits. Cognitively, they may struggle with indecisiveness and difficulty remembering things or concentrating.

Your loved one may also exhibit physical signs such as lethargy, slowed movements, unexplained aches and pains that do not go away with standard treatments, and fatigue. It is important to look out for red flags, such as talk about death, self-harm, or suicide. These red flags should not be ignored. They need immediate attention.

Practice listening Listen to your loved one without judgment. Allow them to talk without needing to jump in immediately to fix things. Acknowledge their pain and experiences, reassuring them that it is okay for them to feel as they do. Do not minimize their feelings by sharing sentiments such as “Others have it worse than you,” or “Just cheer up; it will be okay soon enough.”

Be present There are many ways for you to be present for your loved one, including checking in regularly, even if it is a simple text message or a call that helps them to feel loved and less alone. You can also offer practical support through gestures such as helping with errands, cooking them a meal, or accompanying them when they have an appointment with their doctor or therapist.

Don’t take things personally When you interact with a depressed person, their mood can affect you, particularly their irritability or withdrawal. This is not a reflection of what they think of you. The illness does strange things to people and how they respond to others. Remember that in those moments you are tempted to take their behavior personally.

Take a measured approach It is easy to become overly responsible for a depressed loved one’s well-being. Their depression can pull you away from your own life, and you can also feel guilty when you cannot always help them. Boundaries are important, as is the reminder that your love, presence, and support are a part of the puzzle, but they are not the whole solution.

Taking a measured approach means reminding yourself that by stepping back to allow them greater independence and not neglecting your own needs, you are also caring for yourself. This enables you to show up better for them as well. You do the most good for a depressed person when you are consistent and compassionate toward them, balancing that with taking adequate care of yourself.

Encourage them to seek help Depression requires the intervention of professionals, and you should not take the load on yourself. Do not pressure or nag them, whether it is to attempt to tell them to snap out of it, or to go see a therapist. This will only serve to increase their feelings of guilt and perhaps even resistance to the idea of getting help. Rather, you can gently guide your depressed loved one toward a therapist or counselor for the help they need.

Helping a Depressed Person

Depression is a significant challenge, but one that can be overcome. You can effectively come alongside a depressed loved one to help them as they face this challenge. Love and nurture them in a wise, healthy, and balanced way. This requires understanding what depression is and how it works, being present for them within healthy limits, and encouraging them to seek professional help.

Whether you are looking for support in this process or for a resource for someone who is depressed, a Christian counselor can help. Connect with a counselor today to get started.

item.title: Perfectionism and Anxiety: Is Pride Just Insecurity in Disguise?
item.description:
Some of the most prideful people are often the most insecure. There’s a common misconception that prideful people are bold, arrogant, and think quite highly of themselves. Of course, this is true in many cases, but it may not be typical.

More often, pride comes out of insecurity. Pride manifests in the places where people are the most unsure of themselves or are the most afraid of being exposed. Pride really shines in those fragile parts of their lives where they’re the most desperate for approval.

Pride and insecurity might look like opposites on the surface, but if you dig deep enough, you’ll find that they often share the same root. Someone who is insecure will often try to prove that they are worthy. Outwardly, this looks like confidence, but it’s actually more of a defense mechanism.

Insecure Pride as a Defense

Pride can be difficult to spot sometimes because it wears a lot of different masks. One of those masks is defensiveness. In the real world, this might look like someone’s need to win every argument or to be looked upon as the smart one in the friend group. It could also manifest as a refusal to apologize or to admit weakness. Sometimes it even shows itself as perfectionism and anxiety.

Someone who appears prideful might actually feel inadequate, and they might become highly critical of others. If they can’t measure up to the accomplishments of someone else, they might criticize and try to bring that person down to their level.

Prideful people also have a difficult time apologizing or admitting their own mistakes. They might cover up their failings or try to project them onto someone else. This can manifest as phrases such as “You made me do it” or “If you hadn’t done that, I wouldn’t have done this.” Prideful people rarely take responsibility for their own failures because they don’t want to add another mistake to what they believe is an already lengthy list of their flaws.

As destructive as they are, prideful behaviors are sometimes praised and admired because they can look quite attractive. They might look like confidence to the world, a trait often praised in our society. This praise reinforces the behavior because it also feeds the person’s ego. This creates a cycle of behavior. But when you look a little deeper, under the fake confidence, you will likely see that these behaviors are protecting fragile self-esteem.

The Cycle of Pride

When someone fears being rejected, they might present themselves as superior in an attempt to convince themselves and their audience of their worth. Because they don’t believe they can meet someone else’s standard, they puff themselves up, trying to appear better than others.

Pride and insecurity are both part of a larger cycle. Insecurity creates a fear of exposure. Protective pride in the form of arrogance or perfectionism creates a temporary ego boost, which pressures you to maintain this false mask. And the knowledge that you’re falsely elevating yourself or are inauthentically being propped up by others creates even deeper insecurity.

Pride in the Bible

The Bible has quite a lot to say about pride. Scripture consistently warns that pride can lead to a destructive path. Proverbs 16 tells us plainly that “Pride goes before destruction, a haughty spirit before a fall.” (Proverbs 16:18, NIV)

What does pride mean in this context? In this passage, pride does not refer to confidence or feeling good about yourself. Feeling confident in the creation God made you to be is not a detriment, but a goal. Biblically speaking, pride refers to an inflated view of oneself that pushes God and others out of their proper place. It is a posture of the heart that believes it’s better than anyone and doesn’t need correction.

The Hebrew word used here in Proverbs for pride is gaon. At its core, it means height or majesty. When used negatively, as it is in this context, it refers to an inflated view of oneself that pushes God and others out of their proper place. It’s the idea of rising above others in a falsely elevated way.

This can happen through arrogance, prideful elevation of oneself, self-exaltation, or a sense of superiority. Proverbs 16:18, in the original text, also uses a related idea, ruach gavoah, which means a high or lofty spirit. Together, these terms paint a picture of someone who has lifted themselves to appear more important than they actually are.

Having pride has become a badge of honor in modern culture. Biblically, elevation belongs to God, not us. By puffing up (gaon), we create an attitude that eventually causes the fall that Proverbs warns about.

Scripture also helps us understand that pride can hide insecurity. In Luke 18, Jesus tells a story about two men who went to the temple to pray. One was a Pharisee, a man who would have been respected in his day for his religious devotion. The other was a tax collector, someone whom most of his contemporaries would have called corrupt.

The Pharisee prayed confidently: “‘God, I thank you that I am not like other people, robbers, evildoers, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week and give a tenth of all I get.’” (Luke 18:11-12, NIV)

The tax collector took an opposite posture. Scripture says he stood at a distance and wouldn’t even look up to heaven. He didn’t have a long and eloquent prayer, but simply said, “God, have mercy on me, a sinner.” (Luke 18:13, NIV)

The result might surprise you. The tax collector, not the prideful Pharisee, went home justified before God (Luke 18:14) because the tax collector was honest. He wasn’t comparing himself to anyone or trying to prove his worth. He simply admitted his need while the Pharisee was busy defending his own worth.

Pride Is Exhausting

Maintaining an image, like the Pharisee in our example, takes a lot of effort. If your identity depends on appearing strong, capable, or morally superior, then you are constantly attempting to manage how others see you.

Every interaction or conversation, the ones most people don’t give much thought to, becomes heavily important when you are protecting your curated image. Constructive criticism is viewed as an attack, and every mistake is seen as an enemy. That responsibility can be downright exhausting.

God Is Our Peace

What brings peace and can quiet those insecurities and squelch that pride?

Humility is often misunderstood. Many people assume that humility is thinking poorly of yourself. But that’s not biblical humility at all. Humility is simply seeing yourself accurately. It is the ability to recognize your strengths without exaggerating, as well as your weaknesses without cover-up. This accurate self-assessment actually creates emotional freedom.

Humility recognizes grace. When you can admit your frailties, limitations, and mistakes, you leave room for God’s forgiveness and grace. Your IQ, test score, paycheck, or social media presence isn’t going to ever be good enough to get you to Heaven.

“For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith – and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God –  not by works, so that no one can boast.” (Ephesians 2:8-9, NIV) That realization alone can be humbling and remove the need for pride.

Therapy Can Help

Many prideful behaviors stem from old insecurities. Maybe the mistakes you made as a child were harshly criticized or constantly compared to others. Pride then can become a shield or a way to compensate for that lingering sense of inadequacy.

Therapy can help you trace your prideful behaviors back to their roots. When you stop trying to maintain a perfect image, you open yourself up to growth. You can finally deal with the underlying issues. When you do this, something beautiful and authentic happens.

You will begin to feel safe enough to acknowledge your own limitations, fears, or weaknesses. You will find a place of humility. And with this self-actualization, the need for pride and the perfectionism and anxiety that often come with it will start to fade, leaving room for the awesome work God wants to do in you.

If you need help addressing issues of insecurity or pride, call our offices and make an appointment. Specially trained therapists can help you grow in your humility and embrace the grace of a God who does not require perfection.

item.title: How to Keep Your Children from Inheriting Your Trauma
item.description:
Most parents want to give their kids the world, not their trauma. They want to make their life easier, surprise them with much-desired gifts, and set them up for a comfortable and secure future. They want to make sure that their legacy lives on in the lives of their offspring, even after they’re gone. They think about homes, heirlooms, and savings accounts that they’ll someday pass down, assuring their children will get what is rightfully theirs.

This likely sounds like a great undertaking. If we get everything right with no unpredictable events, life will go well for our children. In the real world, this is not possible. Jesus assures us, “In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

Not everything parents pass down fits into a box or a bank account. In all that focus on giving their kids the best, many parents forget something more important. Parents fail to protect their children from experiencing things like their unresolved pain, old wounds, unhealthy patterns, and harmful parenting practices that are excused because it’s how the parent was raised.

As noble as it is to set your children up for a successful future by giving them monetary gifts, it’s more important to be mindful and self-aware of the internal emotions or activators that cause the parent(s) to react vs. respond to a challenge or struggle. Not passing along negative and detrimental behaviors is critical to decreasing the growth of generational wounds, which decrease the quality of life within the family unit. When parents live in the aftermath of trauma, it changes the way they see the world and how they interact with their children. Poor self-awareness of internal negative thoughts and emotional responses can lead to poor judgment, harming the children, and inadvertently creating trauma for the kids.

Being Raised in the Aftermath of Trauma

Realistically, we can’t eliminate big trauma-inducing events from our lives. You will inevitably face big life moments during your children’s formative years. Death of a loved one, financial struggles, marital issues, health scares, and other difficult moments are bound to happen.

Matthew 5:45 tells us that rain will fall on both the just and the unjust, meaning that no matter how good a person you are, you will face hardships because you’re human and because we are living in a fallen world.

God never promised that He’d remove major obstacles, just that He’d help us walk through and overcome them. As scary and tense as these events might be, they’re not actually what will mentally and emotionally wound your children. What will cause long-lasting negative consequences is your inability to recognize when you are reacting to these traumas.

Trauma, left unprocessed and unhealed, has a way of shaping the way you react vs. respond to stress. Without deliberate and conscious effort, that response is likely to be unhealthy. Stress and trauma aftermath have a way of chipping away at your patience and creating unreasonable fears that can creep into every aspect of your life. Unfortunately, that includes your parenting.

How Trauma Transfers

Children, whether they’re toddlers or teens, look to you as their guidepost and compass. They watch you. They study how you react or respond, and how you cope. And in those moments of crisis when you feel overwhelmed and ready to fall apart, they’re watching.

When you don’t even realize that you’re teaching, you’re showing them how to speak to themselves and how to respond to others, even those who’ve been hostile toward them. You’re showing them how to handle difficult moments, and without even realizing it, they will begin to mirror these actions.

You can also inadvertently transfer your pain and woundedness directly, not just by your example of self-regulation, but by how you treat them during a crisis. Beyond just watching and learning from your example, you’re also molding your child(ren) through your actions.

It’s great if you have composure amid adversity, but sometimes that strength can also make you behave in ways that appear hostile or emotionally unavailable. While you might be handling the crisis itself like a boss, the stress of the situation may appear in more subtle ways. Your tone with them might become sharper or your patience short. You might unconsciously emotionally shut down or place unreasonable expectations on your child.

Though they may seem unrelated and relatively small compared to the big crisis you’re juggling, these subtle but toxic moments can leave a lasting imprint on your child, which may even injure your relationship with them.

How To Interrupt the Transfer

No parent intends to traumatize their child/children. You don’t want to transfer your past or present woundedness to your child, but how do you prevent it? You’ve taken the first step in preventing it by reading this article. By recognizing that trauma can transfer to your child, you are making steps toward preventing it.

How exactly it is transferring may be a little more difficult to decipher because trauma doesn’t always manifest in obvious ways. Yelling or complete emotional withdrawal are easier to identify and control, but subtle trauma responses are often just as damaging.

They show up in patterns such as emotional dysregulation, constant tension, overprotectiveness, emotional unavailability, or inadvertently placing your fears and insecurities onto your child. Children are incredibly perceptive and sense stress incredibly well. They often internalize it even when they don’t verbalize it. Young children are not equipped with the emotional vocabulary to verbalize their feelings, nor are some adults.

To interrupt trauma transfer, ask yourself if you’re reacting out of fear, unresolved anger, grief, or another pain in your past. Am I projecting my anxieties, fears, or overthinking onto my child?

Research shows that children of parents who’ve experienced significant unresolved woundedness, anger, resentment, bitterness, and trauma memories are two to three times more likely to develop anxiety, depression, or PTSD (Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder). Chronic parental stress can also affect a child’s emotional regulation, alter stress hormone levels, and increase vulnerability to mental health challenges.

The good news is that by recognizing your unresolved trauma responses and identifying negative behavioral patterns in yourself, you can actively work on processing your trauma properly.

Therapy

While you can do some of the work yourself, in trying to identify your negative behavioral patterns and what is triggering (activating) them, it’s wise to employ the help of a professional Christian therapist. In therapy, you can work on resolving your own trauma or the ones that you’ve inherited. You can learn to identify how to become more self-aware of your internal struggles in your thoughts, emotions, and what your body is holding and where it holds it. Identify where you hold anger, anxiety, and bitterness in your body. Seek to grow in self-awareness regarding the responses you’re exhibiting that could be impacting your children.

With the help and guidance of a professional therapist, you can then deal with it. And you can also develop healthier coping mechanisms with Cognitive Behavioral Therapy and trauma-focused therapy. You can invite God into the equation, too. Your therapist can point out Scriptures and use biblical principles that can help you interrupt negative and destructive patterns.

By recognizing your responses, the behavior you exhibit in front of your children, and your triggers (those things that cause those behaviors), you can respond intentionally rather than react impulsively. Consistently applying coping strategies will help you break from harmful patterns and give you the skills to create newer, healthier, and more productive ones. You can experience a healthier YOU, a healthier family, more peace and joy, and tools to improve the legacy of your family.

The benefits go way beyond you living a better life. In doing the work now to heal, you are creating a more emotionally safe environment for your children, ensuring they inherit the family heirlooms, not trauma.

God and Trauma

Maybe you inherited old pain and old patterns from long-ago trauma. Maybe you’re still haunted by choices made long before you were born. The Bible doesn’t ignore the fact that trauma can pass from generation to generation. In Exodus 20, God warns of the consequences of sin and brokenness. While they can and often do ripple through families, He promises redemption and healing to those who turn to Him.

This means that while a legacy of pain can affect you, you can heal from it. It also means that it doesn’t have to affect your children and their children. Just as you want to pass down homes, heirlooms, and savings to your children, you also have the power to pass along faith, wisdom, and emotional health.

When you address your own woundedness and lean on God for guidance, you ensure that what you leave behind is a healthy legacy of restoration, redeeming and refreshing the soul. With God, you can create a firm foundation for generations to come.

Learn how to break free from unresolved woundedness and pain through Christian counseling. Contact our reception team today to learn more.

item.title: The Real Reason You Constantly Feel Guilty
item.description:
Some people go through their entire lives feeling guilty, without ever feeling as if they can atone for their mistakes or be fully forgiven and accepted. Guilt can be a helpful response to something. When you make a mistake, your moral compass tries to steer you back to your values with a sense of guilt and shame. Usually, these emotions are resolved when you make things right.

When guilt and shame persist for years, that’s a sign that something is stuck. Guilt that persists for years and decades, however, is not a prolonged attack of conscience. Feelings of constant guilt are your body’s default way of trying to keep you safe. You can resolve persistent guilt, but it will require you to be vulnerable with someone.

Your Conscience as Your Guide

To understand why you constantly feel guilty, you must understand what appropriate guilt looks and feels like, and then compare it with your experience of feeling guilty. Appropriate guilt doesn’t persist for years or decades. It is an immediate cognitive response that acts as a motivator to change the situation, and usually it is clearly connected with wrongdoing.

Let’s say that there is a coworker whom you dislike. One day, you are talking about this coworker with another friend at work, saying unkind things about them and laughing cruelly. You discover that they have walked into the room behind you and have heard you mocking them. Even though you dislike them, you will still likely feel terrible about having been caught in the act of being mean about them.

In a scenario like this, guilt is a response to being caught behaving badly. It is appropriate and will likely motivate you to apologize and perhaps even amend your working relationship with this person.

Appropriate guilt is a logical response to wrongdoing. Once you have done the work to resolve the issue and make amends, that guilty feeling should subside and make way for other emotions like relief, gratitude, and determination to avoid further wrongdoing. In this way, it’s a helpful emotion. What happens when you can’t stop feeling guilty, though?

A Frozen Nervous System

You can’t think yourself out of feeling guilty, and positive affirmations can’t make you feel better. This is because persistent guilt is not an emotion you need to process, nor is it a thought you need to challenge. Constant guilt is a sign that you don’t feel emotionally safe.

In the example of being caught gossiping about your coworker, you had a physical response to being caught in the middle of wrongdoing. In that moment, you were suddenly unsafe because one of your flaws was exposed. That might have affected your reputation in the workplace, your friend’s reputation, or even your job itself. Guilt motivated you to take action by apologizing, so that you could feel safe again.

Persistent guilt and shame often stem from childhood experiences of constantly being criticized, and it is often attached to conditions like OCD, trauma, depression, and perfectionism. It might be stored in your mind as memories or a harsh inner voice constantly criticizing you. It cannot be resolved in your thoughts alone. Persistent guilt is stored in your body, and the only way it can be resolved is to feel safe, seen, accepted, understood, and loved.

The Fig Leaf

In the book of Genesis, we are told that Adam and Eve’s first actions after eating the forbidden fruit were to make fig leaf coverings to hide their nakedness. After that, they hid when God came looking for them. Guilt always combines with shame. This causes us to cover up and hide ourselves away from connection and relationships, especially with those who know us best.

Covering up or isolating yourself will not help. This is not how we feel safe. If anything, isolating yourself will make you feel less safe as you cut off your much-needed emotional support.

You might constantly feel guilty because you were told throughout childhood that there was something flawed about you. Your parents might have been your first bullies, and you have been covering up your authentic self for decades. When you mask important parts of yourself like this, others can’t see you, accept you, or validate you.

You might feel guilty because you do not allow yourself to be seen by others. The only way you will stop feeling guilty all the time is when you are exposed and vulnerable to someone. You need to allow them to validate and love you for being exactly who you are.

Your nervous system will only come out of panic mode, and your guilt will only be resolved, when you can be vulnerable with someone who remains steady and shows you complete acceptance. Only then will you be able to drop your defenses and pretenses, stop performing or trying to earn love, and accept your flaws.

When this happens, your nervous system learns that it is possible to feel safe, possibly for the first time. You’re not perfect; you will make mistakes in the future, but you don’t have to be perfect to be seen, accepted, and loved. This is what safety feels like.

Signs You’re Moving Away from Constantly Feeling Guilty

When you feel safe, you don’t have to continue monitoring yourself, masking your behavior, or keeping your opinions to yourself. You can express your thoughts and state your preferences. You don’t have to hide behind a carefully constructed mask of politeness and peacekeeping. It’s not about acting out-of-character; this is you being your authentic self.

One of the signs that you are resolving your guilt is that you stop apologizing. Before, you were likely apologizing for everything, even when you were doing nothing wrong. When you’re not feeling guilty all the time, you will stop apologizing as if everything is always your fault.

On the other hand, without persistent guilt, you can take accountability for your mistakes and own up to your failures. Sometimes, persistent guilt causes you to cover up your mistakes or gaslight your way out of issues. When you can feel appropriate guilt for your wrongs, you can make amends whenever necessary, without your feelings getting overwhelmed by the incident.

Most importantly, you will know that you have left persistent guilt behind when that harsh inner critic is finally silenced. Perhaps it was an echo of your mother or father’s voice, always criticizing, demeaning, and mocking your every action. Maybe it was your own voice telling you that you were constantly getting things wrong.

When you have stopped feeling guilty all the time, you will only hear that voice occasionally, and usually only when you have done something that can be resolved. Even better than the inner critic voice being silenced, however, is when you begin hearing a small whisper that tells you, “Good job,” “Well done,” and “You deserve good things.”

You may have carried guilt and shame for the longest time, without knowing why and without knowing how to be free. You don’t have to continue like this, but you can’t go on alone. When you meet someone who keeps calm, steady, and accepting when you are vulnerable, you will find the guilt fades. There are people in the world who want to see you, validate you, and love you.

When you go for counseling, you get to be yourself with someone who will never judge you. For many people, this is the first time they have ever felt seen, understood, and validated. If you would like to begin meeting with a counselor, we can help. Please consult our online catalog or speak with our reception team to find someone who can help you overcome persistent guilt.

item.title: Life After a Miscarriage: How to Handle Grief
item.description:
It should be the most exciting moment of your life. You wake up, maybe feeling extra tired, maybe a little nauseous or sore, and you take a test. And then the two pink lines pop up, and whether you’ve prayed for this baby for years, were cautiously hopeful after previous losses, or were surprised by an unexpected pregnancy, you’re going to be a mom.

It’s everything you’ve dreamed. Or maybe you’re unsure, but you’re secretly excited. Whatever the emotion, you take the next step and call the doctor, but they can’t fit you in for another month. So what do you do?

Some women test obsessively, looking for a line progression that gets darker. Other women get blood draws to measure their hormone levels. And others are so confident that they just accept the one test and go into their first ultrasound appointment without a single worry.

And then it hits you. Maybe the hormones aren’t rising, and the levels are actually getting lower, or maybe you’re unaware until the ultrasound wand is on your belly and the doctor says the words you dread to hear: There’s no heartbeat.

And then it’s like everything stops. Your heart is pounding loud enough that you’re sure the doctor and the other customers in the waiting room can hear it, and maybe even you want to be a little sick.

You still feel pregnant. You’re exhausted and sore. You’re craving ice cream and onion rings. But there’s no baby.

So you go home, throw away the line of pregnancy tests with the progressing lines. Put away the clothes you maybe bought for an announcement, and wait for the inevitable. The dreams of a baby shower died, and the hope and confidence you had about being a mom are gone. But it’s not your fault.

The Truth

The truth is that one in four women will miscarry in their first trimester. Sometimes it has to do with a woman’s health, but often it’s just luck. Chromosomal abnormalities are the biggest cause, and there’s not much anyone can do about them. You can test and figure out why, but even if answers come, it doesn’t change the ache that you feel from having lost your child. So how do we go on?

Grief isn’t linear. There are stages, and I’m sure we’ve all heard of them: Anger, denial, bargaining, depression, and acceptance. Sometimes we feel all of these things at once. Sometimes we don’t feel any of them. It depends on the person.

The good news is that we have Jesus to lean on. Scripture tells us that the Lord is near to the brokenhearted. Throughout the Gospels, we also see Jesus weep with those who grieve, reminding us that He is not distant from our suffering.

What can you do?

The most important thing in this process is not to isolate yourself. It may feel like people may not understand, but that does not mean that they can’t be there for you. Whether that is sitting in silence with you, listening to you talk about the dreams you had for your baby and life, or binge- watching your favorite TV show.

You must take care of yourself during this time. Standing in the shower is better than not doing anything to maintain hygiene. Crackers and cheese is better than starving yourself. Be kind to yourself. Your body is going through a lot. The combination of physical exertion and mental turmoil can really wear a body down.

If you are unable to be around people who have children, that is okay. You’re not selfish for your grief, and you aren’t ruining anything. It’s possible to be both happy for a family who announces a pregnancy and sad at the same time.

Scriptures to Help

The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit. – Psalm 34:18

There is nothing that Jesus did not experience and that includes the grief that comes with losing a loved one. Even knowing Lazarus would soon walk out of the tomb, Jesus still wept alongside Mary and Martha. He entered into their grief rather than dismissing it. If Jesus is the same yesterday, today, and forever, then it is true that He is there grieving and mourning with us.

Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. – Matthew 5:4

We can hold onto that promise. We can trust that God will either comfort us Himself or send those to bring us comfort.

He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. – Psalm 147:3

God is so good, and so gracious, that even in the midst of our grief, he brings healing. For some women, healing eventually includes another pregnancy. For others, the road looks quite different. Whatever your story becomes, God’s faithfulness does not depend on the outcome.

Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands. – Isaiah 49:15-16a

God never forgets us, and He feels our pain. We are always cherished and remembered by Him.

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God. – 2 Corinthians 1:3-4.

In our pain, we can remember that Jesus is the source of our comfort, and because we have Him we are able to extend that comfort to others. We don’t know why miscarriage happens, but we do know that everything can be used for our testimony of God’s goodness.

For his anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning. – Psalm 30:5

Grief won’t always feel as overwhelming as it does today. The ache may remain, but God promises that sorrow will not have the final word.

Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you; he will never permit the righteous to be moved. – Psalm 55:22

Remember that there are burdens we pick up that we were never meant to carry. Pain, sorrow…they are only supposed to last for a short time. Lean on the Lord in these hard times. Even if that looks like sobbing on the bathroom floor, asking why, and being angry. It’s okay to be angry.

If all you can bring Him is tears, then bring tears. He never asks us to appear put together. He does not expect perfection. He just wants us to seek His face and presence.

He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away. – Revelation 21:4

Jesus will come back. Scripture says that He catches every tear in a bottle. Revelation says that He will wipe our tears away. What a God!

Whether you carried your baby for two weeks, eight weeks, or experienced a stillbirth, the loss of a child fundamentally changes a woman. There is no “right” way to heal, and moving through the pain is often easier said than done. You don’t have to pretend you’re okay when you’re not. God is faithful to walk with you whether you cry all day, every day, or feel as though you’ve run out of tears.

Next Steps

If you’re struggling with your loss, know that you don’t have to carry it alone. At Seattle Christian Counseling, we provide a confidential, safe place where you can grieve honestly, ask the hard questions, and heal at your own pace. Whether your loss was recent or feelings from years ago are resurfacing, we’d be honored to walk alongside you on your healing journey.

item.title: How to Begin Improving Mental Health for Moms Running on Empty
item.description:
As mothers, we take on more responsibility and roles than other people in our families’ lives. We often play the role of maid, chef, chauffeur, teacher, nurse, event coordinator, and disciplinarian. If you lead a Christian home, then you are also the spiritual leader, drawing your family closer to Christ.

With these responsibilities, you may inevitably begin to experience burnout, anxiety, depression, or fatigue. Learning the ways to improve mental health can help you get back on track to being the Christian mother you are.

Ways to Improve Mental Health for Moms

When you feel overwhelmed, knowing ways to improve mental health can alleviate the burden. Why do we as mothers believe that we must shoulder life’s problems on our own? Are we afraid it will make us appear weak or as if we cannot manage our family?

More women lose themselves in the process of raising their children. Busyness is a snare. How many times have you said, “I don’t have time to do that”? What if we removed that phrase from our vocabulary and focused on setting boundaries to protect what is most important, such as our relationships, peace, and mental health?

Try the following ways to improve mental health to bring peace of mind, lower stress, and prioritize what is truly important.

Ask for help

Starting today, why not ask for support from those around you? Your spouse, parent, sibling, friend, or neighbor could be the answer to your delegation of responsibilities. For example, you could ask a trusted mom friend to care for your children while you run a few errands, and you will repay in kind. If you have a church family or a mom group, you may be able to ask for support with specific tasks.

Matthew 11:28 states, “Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.” Sometimes God sends special individuals into our lives to assist us. As I think about asking for help, I recall an internet story from years ago that spelled out how oblivious we are to accepting help at times.

In the story, the individual needed to be rescued, and they kept calling on God to help them. God sent a villager with a rope to help, and they turned them down, saying, “God will provide. He will help.” Then came two other forms of help, and these were turned down as well. The individual who passes away ends up in heaven and says to God, “Why didn’t you save me?”

God then replies, “I sent multiple methods of help.” Although this story is fictional, it helps us reexamine how God may be speaking to us and how we must attune our hearts and minds to really hear from Him.

Most people want to help, but they don’t know what you need. They may not see the need as clearly as you do. Spouses often fall into this category because they see the mother of the family as the one who keeps everything together. Enlisting their help with children, errands, and housework can lower your stress and help you slow down.

Schedule self-care

Forget the spa. Self-care can be whatever activity makes you feel more like yourself. Self-care should provide you with a mental lift and bring joy to your spirit. For some mothers, this can look like grabbing a coffee from the local café and sitting at a table to enjoy it. For others, it can be indulging in a hobby, such as crocheting, crafts, reading, or painting.

Self-care should happen every day. This could be a five-minute facial mask before bed, painting your nails, or curling up with a novel. Self-care can include reaching out to others, like calling your best friend or sister to chat. Aim for at least 5 to 15 minutes a day to do something just for you.

Prioritize sleep

Staying up late might help to get little Johnny’s school project done, but it won’t help lower your stress. Plus, sleep deprivation sets the tone for the next day and triggers the fight-or-flight response. Your mind and body need good-quality sleep to process emotions and support bodily functions.

It can be challenging to get enough sleep with small children. Ask for help from others, or adopt a bedtime routine for both you and your children. For example, after dinner and kitchen cleanup, give your children baths and read a story before putting them to bed. As soon as they are down, skip the social media scroll and work on your own routine.

Perhaps soak in the tub or take a shower, brew some herbal tea, and go to bed a little earlier. Try changing into pajamas before you make dinner if you shower in the morning. Sometimes, making one adjustment can mean the difference between a good night’s rest and waking up throughout the night.

Make healthy meals

The ingredients in ultra-processed foods impact physical, mental, and emotional health. These chemicals interfere with the brain’s processes and can lead to mental health issues, such as anxiety and depression. Healthier meals for you and your family will improve your health and help you save money.

Look for food items with little to no processing. Whole foods like meat, fresh fruits and vegetables, whole grains, and healthy fats are often more cost-effective in the long run. Check out easy cookbooks if you are new to menu planning and cooking or speak to a nutritionist if you are not sure what types of meals would be best.

The library offers a great selection of cookbooks. Through Google or Pinterest, you can type the ingredients you have, and meal ideas will populate. Additionally, you can type in “Give me a four-ingredient meal” on Pinterest or use some of the AI websites, such as ChatGPT or Gemini, and receive results. You can also use prompts such as, “Give me an affordable meal plan to feed a family of three.” These resources are helpful.

Focus on fitness process

Most people give up an exercise regimen because it feels daunting. They end up dreading it, or they don’t see a difference on the scale right away. This can lead to feelings of defeat and frustration. Yet exercise releases endorphins that activate the parasympathetic nervous system and reduce stress hormones.

Instead of focusing on the outcome, such as losing weight, a number on the scale, or fitting into a dress, try focusing on the daily process. What activities make you feel good? Maybe take your children for a stroll outside, try a dance video at home, or practice Pilates. Think about family activities as well, such as bicycling, hiking, and swimming.

Go outside

Sometimes getting outside and enjoying nature is just what the doctor ordered, especially if you live in a colder climate with fewer hours of daylight. Sunlight has been proven to boost mood and regulate emotions. Natural light can trigger the release of serotonin, a neurotransmitter responsible for feelings of happiness and contentment.

Aim to spend time outdoors daily. This could look like sitting on the front step with a cup of coffee or taking a walk. Have a picnic with your children or visit the park. If you can’t get outdoors today, open a window or sit by one to let natural sunlight bathe the room.

Try a 40-day social media fast

The author, Wendy Speake, of The 40-Day Social Media Fast: Exchange Your Online Distractions for Real-Life Devotion, writes about how Christians can get so caught up in the world (and the World Wide Web) that they miss the important things.

Think back to a time before cell phones in our back pockets or in our hands. Were we more productive? Did we spend more quality time doing things that matter to us, our family, and to God? One of the pleas Speake writes about is to “Lift your eyes and find the good works God prepared for you to walk in today.”

When our actions misalign with our values and beliefs, we can feel depressed and anxious. Taking a step back from social media allows you to free your mind, time, and energy for other worthwhile adventures. Try the 40-day social media fast, connecting with God instead of friend requests, and see how you feel at the end.

Speak to a counselor

Sometimes you may not feel like you can share what is really bothering you. Maybe you feel guilty because, as a mother, you think you should be happy and loving 24/7, but instead, you feel stressed out and burned out, snapping at your loved ones.

Counseling can help. A Christian counselor is unbiased and keeps anything you share confidential. They can help you see where you are in this season of life, help you course-correct by addressing your mindset, thoughts, and behaviors, and help you draw closer to God in the process. Try a counseling session or two, either in-office or virtual, to see if it’s a good fit for you.

Christian Counseling to Improve Mental Health

The above suggestions are ways to improve mental health as a stressed-out mom trying to raise her children and enjoy this season of life. Many of these are lifestyle changes or habits you need to adopt to lessen stress, anxiety, and depression. But burnout is real and can make your days challenging.

Christian counseling can introduce you to customized ways to improve mental health by combining faith-based principles with psychological methods. Contact our office today to schedule an assessment.
